newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: Ariane rocket launches switched.
newsitem.headline: Ariane rocket launches switched.

text.p: Problems resulting from the increased production of satellites have forced Europe's Arianespace company to switch the launch order of its next rockets, space officials said on Wednesday.

The 96th Ariane rocket was removed from the final preparation site at the European Space Agency (ESA) launch centre in French Guiana on the northeast coast of South America to make room for its 97th rocket ahead of a planned June 3rd launch.

The two rockets were transported in opposite directions on railway tracks, one to its final preparation site near the launch pad and the other back to a primary assembly building, witnesses said. Both rockets are of the flight-proven Ariane-4 series.
The 96th Ariane rocket was intially due for launch on May 13 carrying the PanAmSat-6 (PAS-6) satellite for satellite operator PANAMSAT based in Greenwich, Connecticut.

But officials said PANAMSAT decided to reschedule the launch because of an investigation by satellite manufacturer Space Systems/Loral into the cause of power decrease on a similar Loral FS-1300 model satellite. PAS-6 is now planned for launch later in the year.
Roger Solari, French Guiana operations director for Arianespace, told Reuters the problem was due to a speed-up in satellite production.
Satellite launchers and manufacturers underestimated the demand for their services and current industry estimates are 30 percent higher than they were three years ago.
"Satellite makers have made commitments to manufacture a satellite in 18 months. This creates difficulties," Solari said.
But he said Arianespace was still confident of meeting its 1997 objective of 11 launches. Only three launches have taken place so far this year.
Arianespace controls about half the commercial satellite launch market with firm orders for the launch of 40 heavy satellites worth an estimated $3.3 billion.
Its closest rival, the International Launch Services company (ILS), launches the American Atlas rocket series and Russia's Proton rocket.

New satellite launchers are due enter the market next year including a new more powerful version of the McDonnell Douglas Delta rocket and Sea Launch, a floating launch base built by a consortium led the U.S. aerospace giant Boeing.

The first launch of the more powerful, new generation Ariane-5 ended in failure last June when the Western European rocket exploded 37 seconds into flight. A second Ariane-5 launch is now scheduled for mid-September at the earliest.
